phase1.intro:
An interface is a pure contract — it says what a class must be able to do, without saying how.

What should we cover first?

topics.buttonText: What exactly is inside an interface?
dialogue: Every method inside an interface is `public abstract` by default (no body at all), and every field is implicitly `public static final` — meaning fields on an interface are really just shared constants, not per-object state.
`class Circle implements Drawable, Resizable` is Circle signing two separate contracts at once. [[key:Unlike extending a class, a class can implement as many interfaces as it wants]].

stickyNote.definition: Interface methods are public abstract by default; fields are public static final constants. A class can implement any number of interfaces.

topics.buttonText: What are default and static methods on an interface?
dialogue: Since Java 8, interfaces got two extra tricks: [[term:default methods]] give a method an actual body right on the interface, which any implementing class inherits automatically unless it chooses to override it.
And [[term:static methods]] on an interface — like `Drawable.info()` — belong to the interface itself, called exactly like a static method on a class.

stickyNote.flavor: 🎁 a body right on the interface itself
stickyNote.definition: Default methods give an interface method an actual body, inherited automatically. Static methods belong to the interface and are called like Interface.method().

topics.buttonText: When should I use an interface instead of an abstract class?
dialogue: [[key:Interfaces describe capabilities — what a class CAN do — while abstract classes describe what a class IS, complete with shared state]]. If unrelated classes need to share a single behavior, interfaces are usually the better fit.

stickyNote.definition: Interfaces describe what a class CAN do (capability). Abstract classes describe what a class IS, with shared state and fields.

phase2.errorMessage:
Circle.java:10: error: draw() in Circle cannot implement draw() in Drawable
    void draw() {
         ^
  attempting to assign weaker access privileges; was public
1 error
phase2.explanation:
[[warn:Interface methods are implicitly public, and when a class implements one, it has to match that access level exactly]] — never something weaker. Circle wrote `void draw()` with no modifier at all, which defaults to package-private — a step down from the `public` the interface actually requires.

[[key:Java calls this "assigning weaker access privileges" and refuses to compile it]] — you're not allowed to implement a contract with less visibility than the contract promised. The fix is just adding the modifier back: `public void draw()`.

phase3.openingDialogue: Interfaces are contracts — sign them and deliver! 📋

mcq.question:
How many interfaces can a single Java class implement?

A) Exactly one
B) At most two
C) As many as it wants
D) Zero — only abstract classes can be implemented

phase4.selfChallenge:
Create an interface Playable with:
• void play()
• default void stop() — prints "Stopping playback"

Create MusicPlayer and VideoPlayer classes that implement Playable:
• MusicPlayer: play() prints "Playing music 🎵"
• VideoPlayer: play() prints "Playing video 🎬"

In main, create both and call play() and stop() on each.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: default methods weren't added to Java 8 just for convenience — they were actually a rescue plan. Oracle wanted to add new methods like forEach() to old interfaces like List, but doing that the old way would've broken every class that already implemented List without that method. Default methods let them add new interface methods without breaking a decade of existing code.
phase5.openingDialogue: One more thing before you sign more contracts~
